2025-03-23T10:31:52.content:
I'm still awake. Of course I'm still awake. My eyes burn from staring at this laptop screen for the past four hours, scrolling through co-op listings that all seem to want experience I don't have yet. How does anyone get their first position when every posting demands "minimum 1-2 years experience"? Yesterday's career advisor meeting was less than helpful—generic advice about "networking" and "polishing my resume" without any concrete steps. Tomorrow (technically today since it's already past midnight) I have that group presentation for Chen's class at 11, which I'm barely prepared for, and then two back-to-back labs until 6. When am I supposed to find time to apply for these positions? The deadline for priority co-op applications is next Friday, just eight days away. Eight days to somehow transform myself into an ideal candidate.

The apartment is completely silent except for my roommate's occasional snoring through the wall and the hum of my laptop fan that seems to get louder every night. My coffee went cold hours ago, but I just took another sip anyway because apparently I hate myself. My shoulders are tight from hunching over this screen, and I can feel a headache forming behind my right eye. Classic stress headache. My mood is hovering somewhere between panic and resignation.

Last semester I promised myself I'd be more organized this time around. Laughable now. My planner sits next to me, mocking me with its color-coded system that worked for exactly two weeks before everything spiraled. Right now, I have fifteen browser tabs open—three job applications half-completed, the rubric for tomorrow's presentation, research for next week's paper, and a YouTube video about "How to Ace Your Co-op Interview" that I started but never finished. Future me will somehow need to consolidate all this chaos into something productive.

My parents called yesterday asking how the co-op search was going. I lied and said "great, lots of promising leads!" They're so excited about me potentially landing a position at a big company, constantly mentioning how cousin Emma's internship led directly to her job offer. The pressure feels physical, like something sitting on my chest. Tonight it's especially heavy.
Two months ago, I was concerned but optimistic. One month ago, I was actively searching but still managing my course load. Last week, the anxiety started creeping in around the edges. Now? Full-blown panic that oscillates between frantic activity and paralyzed scrolling. Tomorrow won't be any better with its packed schedule. Next week brings three deadlines plus the co-op application cutoff. And somewhere in all this, I'm supposed to eat, sleep, and maintain some semblance of hygiene and social connection.

The worst part is seeing everyone else seemingly handling it all. Jenna already had her first interview yesterday. Marcus landed a position last week within 24 hours of applying. Are they just better at this? More qualified? Better connected? All of the above, probably.

My desk is a disaster zone—empty coffee mugs, scattered index cards with potential interview talking points, printed job descriptions with highlighted keywords I should somehow incorporate into my resume. The soft glow of my desk lamp creates shadows that make everything look more dramatic than it probably is. Or maybe it's exactly as dramatic as it looks.

My plan for tomorrow feels impossible: wake up at 6:30 to finalize my portion of the presentation, meet with the group at 9 for a run-through, present at 11, rush to consecutive labs, then spend the evening completing two job applications. Saturday is earmarked for working on my research paper due next Wednesday and finishing three more applications. Sunday is for whatever crisis emerges between now and then. There's no room for error, no space for the unexpected.

I keep telling myself that future me will thank present me for pushing through this. That by mid-term break, I might actually have a co-op position secured and can focus solely on classes. But present me is exhausted, overwhelmed, and increasingly convinced that I'm not cut out for any of the jobs I'm applying for anyway. The impostor syndrome is deafening tonight.

It's now 2:54 AM. I should sleep. I won't sleep. The cycle continues. One day at a time, one application at a time, one assignment at a time. That's all I can manage right now in this strange liminal space between student life and professional aspirations, between today's deadlines and tomorrow's opportunities, between who I am and who I'm trying to become.

2025-03-23T10:28:26.content: The bass from downstairs literally makes my desk lamp vibrate. I can feel it in my chest. My phone shows Mom called twice—I'll deal with that tomorrow when I don't have to shout over party noise. I'm sitting here in my darkened room, blue laptop light making my face look alien, trying to pretend I'm fine with missing another party. Am I though? FOMO is real tonight. My roommate's laugh echoes up the stairwell—she's probably heading out with everyone else. Earlier today I swore I'd work on that essay for Morrison's class, but all I've done is type my name and stare at the blinking cursor. Tomorrow's study group looms—I promised Taye I'd have the first section outlined. Haven't started. Sunday stretches empty and full of possibility that I'll probably waste scrolling TikTok. The music downstairs changes to something slower. People will leave soon. My mood keeps shifting between relief (thank god I'm not making small talk right now) and regret (but maybe it would be fun?). I exist between yesterday's promises and tomorrow's obligations, not really doing either justice. Last weekend was the same. Next weekend probably will be too. The weekend people are posting on Instagram seems better than mine. Is it though? Maybe they're all just pretending too. My thoughts are scattered like my notes across this desk. I should sleep soon, but the night feels unfinished somehow. Like I'm missing something important happening somewhere else while I'm just... here. Suspended between what was and what will be.

2025-03-23T10:27:54.content: The fluorescent lights buzz overhead like angry wasps trapped in glass. God I'm tired. TIRED. My eyes burn from staring at these chem formulas for what feels like forever. Three hours left until this thing is due and my coffee sits forgotten, cold and useless beside me. I can smell someone's Chinese takeout mixing with that dusty library book smell and it's making me nauseous. Or maybe that's just the anxiety. Yesterday feels like a dream—why didn't I start this earlier? Future me is always screwed by present me's decisions. Right now everything is just this assignment, these formulas, this moment of pure academic hell. Tomorrow's 8am class looms like a threat. I feel both wired and exhausted, determined yet defeated. The shadows through the windows grow longer as night settles in completely. Other students around me look equally miserable—we're all in this collective suffering bubble. Will I ever learn? Will next week be different? Doubtful. But I keep telling myself that future me will be more organized, even though present me knows that's a beautiful lie I tell myself every single week. Somehow I'll survive until Friday. That's what I keep repeating. Just make it to Friday. The weekend feels impossibly far away, like looking at the horizon from the bottom of a well. One page at a time. One formula at a time. One hour at a time. That's all I can manage right now in this fluorescent purgatory.

2025-03-23T10:28:12.content: Orange light seeps through my blinds. Everything looks soft and unreal. I'm oddly calm despite knowing what's coming today. The tea warms my throat and I can hear absolutely nothing except birds arguing outside my window. Campus is still sleeping. I'm not. My mind keeps jumping between the presentation in four hours and what I'll eat for dinner tonight when this is all over. Anxious but weirdly peaceful too? Yesterday I practiced in front of my mirror until my roommate told me to shut up. Now the words float in my head, rehearsed but still scary. The birds are so LOUD. Why are they so cheerful when I'm sitting here with my stomach in knots? Last week's feedback from Dr. Simmons keeps echoing—"more eye contact, fewer filler words." I'm trying. Really trying. I imagine tonight, how relieved I'll feel, maybe reward myself with something from that bakery near campus. Tomorrow is deliberately empty on my calendar—a gift to future me from present anxious me. The sunlight is growing stronger now, the day accelerating whether I'm ready or not. My tea is getting cold. Just like yesterday's. Just like tomorrow's probably will. Time keeps moving no matter how much I want to freeze this quiet moment before everything gets chaotic. I should review my notes one more time. Will I stumble over the third slide again? Probably. But future me, tonight-me, will have survived somehow. That's the only certainty.
